authors: Swihart SL
title: Colour vision and the physiology of the superposition eye of a butterfly (Hesperiidae)
why: Spectral sensitivity and optics of a skipper's superposition eye; skippers are 12.8 percent of butterfly records and are probably wrong under the butterfly view.
species it would fix: Ancyloxypha; Epargyreus clarus; Hesperiidae; Panoquina ocola; Polites; Urbanus proteus

authors: Horridge GA, Giddings C, Stange G
title: The superposition eye of skipper butterflies
journal or book: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
why: Full paper for the skipper eye (acceptance angle 6 to 8 degrees was logged from the abstract only); would give the sensitivity gain.

authors: Menzel R, Blakers M
title: Colour receptors in the bee eye: Morphology and spectral sensitivity
why: Single-cell recordings in Apis mellifera: UV, blue and green receptors peaking near 350, 440 and 540 nm; the species-level source for the honeybee's Ultraviolet and Red rows.

authors: Srinivasan MV, Lehrer M
title: Spatial acuity of honeybee vision and its spectral properties
why: Behavioural grating acuity of the honeybee (about 0.34 cycles per degree), measured in Apis mellifera's own foragers; gives the Sharpness figure for the most photographed bee and shows acuity rests on the green channel.

authors: Skorupski P, Chittka L
title: Photoreceptor processing speed and input resistance changes during light adaptation correlate with spectral class in the bumblebee, Bombus impatiens
why: Light-adapted integration time of B. impatiens photoreceptors (about 11 ms green, 16 ms UV, 19 ms blue), a species-level measure of how fast a bumblebee eye responds; gives a Speed row value for this species.

authors: Skorupski P, Chittka L
title: Photoreceptor Spectral Sensitivity in the Bumblebee, Bombus impatiens (Hymenoptera: Apidae)
why: Intracellular recordings in B. impatiens itself: UV, blue and green classes with peaks near 347, 424 and 539 nm, which is the species-level measurement for the Ultraviolet row of the common eastern bumblebee.
species it would fix: Bombus bimaculatus; Bombus griseocollis; Bombus impatiens

authors: Straw AD, Warrant EJ, O'Carroll DC
title: A 'bright zone' in male hoverfly (Eristalis tenax) eyes and associated faster motion detection and increased contrast sensitivity
why: Facet size, spatial resolution and temporal-frequency tuning of motion neurons in Eristalis tenax, by sex and by region of the eye; species-level evidence for the drone fly's Sharpness and Speed rows.

authors: Srinivasan MV, Guy RG
title: Spectral properties of movement perception in the dronefly Eristalis
why: Motion neurons of Eristalis tenax peak near 350 nm (UV) and 475 nm for flashes and near 450 nm for moving gratings: a species-level spectral measurement for the drone fly's Ultraviolet row.

authors: Kraatz B, Schmitz L, Frankenburg L, Nelson TJ, Maruta J, Sherratt E
title: A backwards view of visual adaptations: cranial specialization and predator evasion within a cursorial mammal
how to get it: open access likely (Royal Society Open Science); Adelaide repository record
why: Orbit position, vergence and field of view across all leporid genera including Lepus and Sylvilagus; settles eye position and visual field for hare and cottontail. DOI not shown on the record page.

authors: Cervino NG, Elias-Costa AJ, Pereyra MO, Faivovich J.
title: A closer look at pupil diversity and evolution in frogs and toads.
why: Survey of pupil shape across frogs and toads including North American treefrogs and bullfrogs, to settle the horizontal pupil assumption.
species it would fix: Dryophytes cinereus; Dryophytes squirellus; Lithobates catesbeianus; Osteopilus septentrionalis; Rhinella marina

authors: Jander U, Jander R
title: Allometry and resolution of bee eyes (Apoidea)
why: Tabulates eye parameters across many bee species, so it could replace the honeybee's figures with values for bumblebees, carpenter bees and sweat bees.
species it would fix: Agapostemon virescens; Augochlora pura; Bombus impatiens; Megachile; Xylocopa micans; Xylocopa virginica

authors: Rahmoun DE, Lieshchova MA, Gherissi DE, Hadjeris T
title: Anatomical and histological characteristics of the dromedary eye (Camelus dromedarius)
why: Histology of 20 dromedary eyes, ultrasound and iridocorneal angle; retina and lens structure.

authors: Miyazaki T, Naritsuka Y, Yagami M, Kobayashi S, Kawamura K
title: Anatomy and Histology of the Eye of the Nutria Myocastor coypus: Evidence of Adaptation to a Semi-aquatic Life
why: Nutria eye structure: vertical-slit pupil, thin retina without fovea, acuity 1.44-1.58 cpd, photoreceptor density.

authors: Land MF, Nilsson D-E
title: Animal Eyes, 2nd edition, chapters 7 and 8 (apposition and superposition compound eyes)
why: Textbook values for acuity and sensitivity of butterfly, moth, fly and dragonfly eyes, to fill rows no paper in the collection reaches.

authors: Emerling CA
title: Archelosaurian Color Vision, Parietal Eye Loss, and the Crocodylian Nocturnal Bottleneck
why: Gives alligator rod 501 nm and putative RH1 cone 503 nm separately, LWS 535 and 566 double-cone; SWS1 lost, RH2 pseudogenised in crocodylians; turtle opsin complement (Trionychids lose SWS1); parietal eye loss in crocodylians.

authors: Pecsics T, Csörgő T
title: Aspects of cranial adaptation in foot-propelled diving birds: foraging and visual fields of some piscivorous species
why: Estimates horizontal visual field of the anhinga itself, finding the narrowest binocular field of the species compared (cormorant and goosander wider).

authors: Prusky GT, West PWR, Douglas RM
title: Behavioral assessment of visual acuity in mice and rats
why: Behavioural grating acuity of the mouse (visual water task).

authors: Macuda T, Gegear RJ, Laverty TM, Timney B
title: Behavioural assessment of visual acuity in bumblebees (Bombus impatiens)
why: The Common Eastern Bumble Bee's behavioural acuity; would give the bumblebee a measured figure of its own.

authors: Guignard Q, Goodwin JTL, Kimoto T, et al.
title: Characterising spectral sensitivity and the role of sunlight intensity in Japanese beetle (Popillia japonica) behaviour
why: Spectral sensitivity of a scarab met in Florida gardens; the licence says open access, so try the publisher page first.

authors: Porter ML, Kingston AC, McCready R, Cameron EG, Hofmann CM, Suarez L, Olsen GH, Cronin TW, Robinson PR.
title: Characterization of visual pigments, oil droplets, lens and cornea in the whooping crane Grus americana.
why: Only measured crane; would let the sandhill crane borrow pigments and the ultraviolet question inside the genus.

authors: Gilbert BJ
title: Color Vision in the Bovine
why: Operant test of heifers discriminating 450, 535 and 610 nm lights; behavioural colour discrimination in cattle.

authors: Riol JA, Sanchez JM, Eguren VG, Gaudioso VR
title: Colour perception in fighting cattle
why: Behavioural colour test in fighting-bull cattle (Bos taurus); bears on red/green discrimination.

authors: Birgersson J, Alm U, Forkman B
title: Colour vision in fallow deer: a behavioural study
why: Behavioural colour discrimination in fallow deer; checks that a two-cone ungulate in the Cervidae chooses by colour as the deer view assumes.

authors: Barber CL, Prescott NB, Jarvis JR, Le Sueur C, Perry GC, Wathes CM
title: Comparative study of the photopic spectral sensitivity of domestic ducks (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus), turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo gallopavo) and humans
why: Behavioural photopic spectral sensitivity from 326 to 694 nm in domestic (mallard-derived) ducks: peak 544 to 577 nm and UV-A is perceived.

authors: Thomas J. Lisney, Karyn Stecyk, Jeffrey Kolominsky, Gary R. Graves, DOUGLAS R.W. WYLIE, Andrew N. Iwaniuk
title: Comparison of eye morphology and retinal topography in two species of new world vultures (Aves: Cathartidae)
why: Eye size and retinal ganglion cell map of turkey and black vultures, the New World vultures that sit in the bird view; no sharpness exists for either.

authors: Anders Ödeen
title: Complex Distribution of Avian Color Vision Systems Revealed by Sequencing the SWS1 Opsin from Total DNA
why: Sequences for crows, jays, raptors, gulls and others; says which common families are violet type and which ultraviolet type (the 2013 and 2011 papers I opened cite it for Corvidae, Laridae and Falconiformes).
species it would fix: Buteo jamaicensis; Columba livia; Corvus brachyrhynchos; Cyanocitta cristata; Falco sparverius; Larus argentatus

authors: Klećkowska-Nawrot J, Badenhorst S, Borawski W, Goździewska-Harłajczuk K, Aktaş A, Chrószcz A, et al.
title: Descriptive comparative morphology of the eye and ocular adnexa in Felidae: observations from a clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa), African lion (Panthera leo), and Pallas's cat (Otocolobus manul)
why: Lion eyeball shape, tapetum colour (milky blue to blue-green), pupil shape, orbit measurements, from two Angola lions.

authors: Harland DP, Jackson RR, Macnab AM
title: Distances at which jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) distinguish between prey and conspecific rivals
why: Its table of discrimination distances for 37 species, lyssomanines among them, would set how much coarser the Lyssomanes setting should be; the abstract gives only that lyssomanines see shorter.

authors: Hebel R
title: Distribution of retinal ganglion cells in five mammalian species (pig, sheep, ox, horse, dog)
why: Ganglion-cell maps of pig, sheep, ox, horse and dog in one paper: streak and area centralis for the species a deer view is lent to.
species it would fix: Bos taurus; Equus caballus; Ovis aries; Sus scrofa

authors: Rojas LM, McNeil R, Cabana T, Lachapelle P
title: Diurnal and nocturnal visual function in two tactile foraging waterbirds: the American White Ibis and the Black Skimmer
why: Rod and cone density, ganglion cell density and ERG sensitivity in the American white ibis itself (no DOI printed on the PDF; cite by Condor 99:191-200).

authors: Eleanor M. Caves, Esteban Fernández‐Juricic, Laura Ann Kelley
title: Ecological and morphological correlates of visual acuity in birds: supplementary Tables S1 and S2 (acuity, eye size and body mass for 94 species)
how to get it: open-access supplement on the journal page (cc-by); Table S1 download
why: Would give a species-level acuity for every bird in the 94-species table (corvids, a sandpiper, flycatchers, falcons, owls, ducks) in one file; the article text is open and names no per-species values for the common backyard species.
species it would fix: Anas platyrhynchos; Aquila audax; Corvus brachyrhynchos; Cyanocitta cristata; Falco sparverius; Larus delawarensis; Zonotrichia albicollis

authors: Ault SJ
title: Electroretinograms and retinal structure of the eastern screech owl (Otus asio) and great horned owl (Bubo virginianus)
why: Retinal structure and ERG sensitivity in the eastern screech owl and great horned owl themselves (no DOI; open access via SORA PDF).

authors: Ault SJ, House EW
title: Electroretinographic responses of the great horned owl Bubo virginianus
why: ERG spectral and flicker responses in the great horned owl; flicker-related and sensitivity rows (volume and pages not on the BHL page; check the PDF).

authors: Duarte Toledo R (director: Bueno García JM)
title: Estudio de la óptica ocular del bovino de Lidia: Un modelo animal de ojo con tolerancia al desenfoque
how to get it: thesis, open record (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 ES) at Universidad de Murcia Digitum
why: Optics of the bovine eye: hyperopia, little accommodation, elliptical pupil raising depth of focus; supports cattle acuity and pupil rows. Year not on the page.

authors: Anders Ödeen, Olle Håstad, Per Alström
title: Evolution of ultraviolet vision in the largest avian radiation - the passerines: Additional files 1 to 3 (species list with site-90 residue)
how to get it: open-access additional files on the journal page

species it would fix: Agelaius phoeniceus; Caracara plancus; Cardinalis cardinalis; Mimus polyglottos; Sturnus vulgaris

authors: Schott RK, Perez L, Kwiatkowski M, Imhoff V, Gumm JM
title: Evolutionary analyses of visual opsin genes in frogs and toads: Diversity, duplication, and positive selection
why: Opsin genes (RH1, LWS, SWS1, SWS2, no RH2) for 33 North American and other anurans; check species table for bullfrog, Hyla, Anaxyrus, Rhinella.
species it would fix: Anaxyrus terrestris; Hyla cinerea; Lithobates catesbeianus; Rhinella marina

authors: not shown on the page opened (PeerJ article 3145)
title: Evolutionary analysis of vision genes identifies potential drivers of visual differences between giraffe and okapi
why: Giraffe cone opsin genes: SWS1 plus LWS (dichromat), with an A180S substitution expected to shift the L cone about 5 nm toward red; settles giraffe cone classes and opsin genes.

authors: Chatterjee P, Mohan U, Krishnan A, Sane SP
title: Evolutionary constraints on flicker fusion frequency in Lepidoptera
why: Flicker fusion values for many butterflies and moths; would replace one swallowtail's 107 Hz with figures for the Monarch, Gulf Fritillary and Cabbage White.
species it would fix: Agraulis vanillae; Danaus plexippus; Pieris rapae; Vanessa cardui

authors: Kern TJ
title: Exotic Animal Ophthalmology (Chapter 35, Veterinary Ophthalmology, 6th ed., ed. Gelatt KN)
why: Exotic and zoo mammal eyes; may include big cats, giraffe, camels, squirrels per chapter scope (contents not seen).

authors: Wada S, Kawano-Yamashita E, Koyanagi M, Terakita A
title: Expression of UV-sensitive parapinopsin in the iguana parietal eyes and its implication in UV-sensitivity in vertebrate pineal-related organs
why: Green iguana parietal eye holds UV-sensitive parapinopsin plus green-sensitive parietopsin; settles the parietal-eye row for Iguana iguana.

authors: Bergman M, Rutowski RL
title: Eye morphology and visual acuity in the pipevine swallowtail (Battus philenor) studied with a new method of ommatidial mapping
journal or book: Biological Journal of the Linnean Society
why: Would give a measured acuity and ommatidial map for a swallowtail met in Florida; the abstract alone gives no figures.

authors: Lisney TJ, Iwaniuk AN, Bandet MV, Wylie DR
title: Eye shape and retinal topography in owls (Aves: Strigiformes)
why: Eye shape, ganglion cell density, visual streak and fovea measured in great horned owl and barred owl themselves (eastern screech owl not included).

authors: Briscoe AD, Bernard GD
title: Eyeshine and spectral tuning of long wavelength-sensitive rhodopsins: no evidence for red-sensitive photoreceptors among five Nymphalini butterfly species
why: Long-wave pigment peaks (510-534 nm) measured in Nymphalis antiopa, Inachis (Aglais) io, Junonia coenia and Vanessa cardui, plus Pieris rapae for comparison; gives lambda max for four of the top-ranked butterflies.
species it would fix: Aglais io; Junonia coenia; Nymphalis antiopa; Pieris rapae; Vanessa cardui

authors: Braekevelt CR
title: Fine structure of the retinal photoreceptors of the great horned owl (Bubo virginianus)
why: Gives rod:single cone:double cone ratio of about 30:1:2 and a colourless 3 micron oil droplet in the great horned owl.

authors: Martins BC
title: Food and Fiber Animal Ophthalmology (Chapter 30, Veterinary Ophthalmology, 6th ed., ed. Gelatt KN)
why: Eye anatomy of cattle, goat and other food animals: horizontal pupil, tapetum, fundus.

authors: Ofri R, Ekesten B
title: Fundamentals of Animal Vision (Chapter 5, Veterinary Ophthalmology, 6th ed., ed. Gelatt KN)
why: Cross-species tables of visual field, acuity, colour vision and flicker for domestic and some wild mammals; likely covers cattle, goat, camelids.
species it would fix: Bos taurus; Capra hircus; Lama glama

authors: Kelley MD, Caglianone J, Mendonca MT
title: Gopher tortoises behaviorally utilize UV signals in their external environment
how to get it: open access (web abstract; ask authors for a paper)
why: Behavioural choice test: gopher tortoises prefer a UV-containing disc, the only Gopherus polyphemus evidence on UV sensitivity; meeting abstract only (year inferred as 2019, not stated on page).

authors: Cronin TW, Kinloch MR, Olsen GH
title: Head-bobbing behavior in walking whooping cranes (Grus americana) and sandhill cranes (Grus canadensis)
why: Measures the head-bob cycle in walking sandhill cranes: four-step pattern tied to stepping, gaze held still between thrusts, no bobbing when running.

authors: Casey A. Gilman
title: Head-bobs in birds: the eyes have it
why: Commentary on what head-bobbing does for vision; would settle which of the wader view's walkers bob, and whether chickens and pigeons hold the head for the same length of time.
species it would fix: Ardea herodias; Columba livia; Fulica americana; Gallus gallus domesticus; Grus canadensis

authors: Sillman AJ, Ronan SJ, Loew ER
title: Histology and microspectrophotometry of the photoreceptors of a crocodilian, Alligator mississippiensis
journal or book: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 243: 93-98
why: Primary measurement of alligator rod and cone pigments (444, 503, 535, 566 nm) and oil droplets; abstract itself not opened (publisher pages blocked), citation confirmed from reference list of Nagloo et al. 2016.

authors: Peter Olsson, Olle Lind, Mindaugas Mitkus, Kaspar J. V. Delhey, Almut Kelber
title: Lens and cornea limit UV vision of birds – a phylogenetic perspective
how to get it: open-access, Table 1 on the journal page (cc-by); no login

species it would fix: Anas platyrhynchos; Ardea cinerea; Buteo buteo; Cygnus olor; Falco tinnunculus; Haliaeetus albicilla; Milvus milvus

authors: Macuda T, Timney B
title: Luminance and chromatic discrimination in the horse (Equus caballus)
why: Horse luminance and chromatic discrimination: which colours a horse separates.

authors: Briscoe AD
title: Molecular diversity of visual pigments in the butterfly Papilio glaucus
why: Would give the Eastern Tiger Swallowtail's own opsin set and so how many colour classes it can have, which the swallowtail rows now borrow from Papilio xuthus.

authors: Duelli P
title: Movement detection in the posterolateral eyes of jumping spiders (Evarcha arcuata, Salticidae)
why: Speed and size thresholds of the rear side eyes would set the surround's motion detector and its timing.

authors: Keiko Yamamoto, Izumi Furuya, Shigeru Watanabe
title: Near-field visual acuity in Japanese jungle crows (Corvus macrorhynchos)
why: The only crow acuity in the collection; crows and jays are among the commonest birds met and have no measured sharpness in the log.

title: Normal Ocular Structure of Dromedary Camel (Camelus dromedarius): Gross, Ultrasonographic and Computed Tomographic Study
why: Dromedary eye biometry (axial length, lens, vitreous) and gross findings: oval pupil, granula iridica, tapetum reported absent.

authors: Meomartino L, Pasolini MP, Lamagna B, Mennonna G, Auletta L, Murino C, Della Valle G, Esposito L
title: Ocular ultrasonographic and biometric features of European brown hares (Lepus europaeus)
why: Axial eye length and lens/vitreous dimensions of 40 hares; gives the eye size from which acuity can be computed.

authors: Paoul S. Martinez, Caryn E. Plummer
title: Ophthalmology of Crocodilia: Alligators, Crocodiles, Caimans, and Gharials
why: Textbook chapter on the crocodilian eye: pupil, fundus, tapetum and visual streak in alligators and caimans, which would give the alligator rows their own source.

authors: Gionfriddo JR, Hamor RE
title: Ophthalmology of New World Camelids (Chapter 32, Veterinary Ophthalmology, 6th ed., ed. Gelatt KN)

authors: Mitchell G, Roberts DG, van Sittert SJ, Skinner JD
title: Orbit orientation and eye morphometrics in giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis)

authors: Loew ER, Govardovskii VI

authors: Calderone JB, Jacobs GH
title: Regional variations in the relative sensitivity to UV light in the mouse retina

title: Retinal adaptation to dim light vision in spectacled caimans (Caiman crocodilus fuscus): Analysis of retinal ultrastructure

authors: Zurek DB, Nelson XJ

authors: Jacobs GH
title: Scotopic and Photopic Visual Capacities of an Arboreal Squirrel (Sciurus niger)

title: Secondary not subordinate: opsin localization suggests possibility for color sensitivity in salticid secondary eyes
